The [Nippon Professional Baseball](/wiki/Nippon_Professional_Baseball "Nippon Professional Baseball") league was planned to be split into two separate leagues in 1949, and Hiroshima prefecture decided to establish a professional baseball team as part of the reconstruction process after the [atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki](/wiki/Atomic_bombing "Atomic bombing"). The team joined the [Central League](/wiki/Central_League "Central League") in December 1949 as the **Hiroshima Carp**. They were named the Carp after the [koi fish](/wiki/Koi "Koi") that climbed the rapids of [Hiroshima Castle](/wiki/Hiroshima_Castle "Hiroshima Castle"), chosen to signify Hiroshima's rebirth and perseverance following the aforementioned atomic bombings. Said name was put forth by a politician named Noboru Tanigawa, who was the face of Hiroshima's bid. Another name put forward was Greens, after a successful semi-professional team of the same name. Others included Bears, Rainbows, Doves, and morbidly, Atoms. However, all the names were put aside, as Tanigawa was so influential to the team's bid, he always had the final decision.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The team's first home field was a prefecture-funded stadium, and the team's lack of sponsorship made it extremely difficult to recruit players. Manager [Hideichi Ishimoto](/w/index.php?title=Hideichi_Ishimoto&action=edit&redlink=1 "Hideichi Ishimoto (page does not exist)") had to personally scout players just to form a starting lineup. The ragtag team ended up in last place from 1950 to 1951.

The team's lack of funding became an even more serious problem in 1951, and it was proposed by NPB that the team be disbanded, or merge with the [Taiyo Whales](/wiki/Taiyo_Whales "Taiyo Whales") team, which was based in [Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi](/wiki/Shimonoseki,_Yamaguchi "Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi") at the time. Hiroshima citizens strongly protested against disbanding the team, and raised the money needed to keep the team through donations.

According to Hammond, the United States [Drug Enforcement Administration](/wiki/Drug_Enforcement_Administration "Drug Enforcement Administration") later told him that the episode had been a setup, and that local authorities regularly entrap American tourists;[[26]](#cite_note-ll97-26) he spent a weekend in jail. Hammond was released after his father traveled to the Bahamas and paid $3,000 for his son's release.[[26]](#cite_note-ll97-26)

Hammond first publicly mentioned his incarceration in the Bahamas as a guest on a 1998 episode of the radio show *[Loveline](/wiki/Loveline "Loveline")*;[[26]](#cite_note-ll97-26) and again when he returned to *Loveline* in 2000 and 2004,[[29]](#cite_note-29)[[30]](#cite_note-Loveline-30) as well as during an appearance on the [*Opie & Anthony*](/wiki/Opie_and_Anthony "Opie and Anthony") show in 2012.[[31]](#cite_note-Opie-31)

*Star Wars* remains one of the most financially successful films of all time. It earned over $2.5 million in its first six days ($13.6 million in 2025 dollars), including $1.5 million during its first weekend (8.26 million in 2025).[[231]](#cite_note-253)[[232]](#cite_note-254) According to *[Variety](/wiki/Variety_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")*'s weekly box office charts, it was [number one at the US box office](/wiki/List_of_1977_box_office_number-one_films_in_the_United_States "List of 1977 box office number-one films in the United States") for its first three weeks. It was dethroned by *[The Deep](/wiki/The_Deep_(1977_film) "The Deep (1977 film)")*, but gradually added screens and returned to number one in its seventh week, building up to $7-million weekends ($37.2 million in 2025) as it entered wide release, and remaining number one for the next 15 weeks.[[3]](#cite_note-BOM-3) It replaced *Jaws* as the highest-earning film in North America just six months into release, eventually grossing $221.3 million during its initial theatrical run ($1.18 billion in 2025 dollars).[[233]](#cite_note-255)[[234]](#cite_note-256) *Star Wars* entered international release towards the end of the year, and in 1978 became the highest-grossing film of all time worldwide.[[235]](#cite_note-257) Its biggest international market was Japan, where it grossed $58.4 million.[[236]](#cite_note-japan-258)

*Star Wars* was still playing in 38 US theaters fourteen months after its initial release. On July 21, 1978, it was expanded to 1,744 theaters, and set a new US weekend record of $10.2 million.[[237]](#cite_note-259)[[238]](#cite_note-260)[[239]](#cite_note-261) The $43.8 million gross from this expansion brought its total domestic gross to over $265 million. Theatrical re-releases in 1979 ($22.5 million), 1981 ($17.2 million), and 1982 ($18 million) brought its cumulative gross in the US and Canada to $323 million, and extended its global earnings to $530 million.[[240]](#cite_note-262)[[241]](#cite_note-263)[[242]](#cite_note-264) *Star Wars* had become the first film to gross $500 million worldwide,[[243]](#cite_note-265)

The leading cause of death in both males and females is lung cancer, which contributes to 26.8% of all cancer deaths.
